definition: Quantify means to measure something and express it as a number or definite amount.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word quantify. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know quantify should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The insurer asked her to quantify the flood damage, so the vague 'we lost almost everything' became a nine-page inventory totaling $48,200.
Gauge is looser than quantify: gauging settles for a feel — 'about thirty, maybe' — while quantifying isn't finished until an actual number is on the page.
Enumerate goes past quantify: quantifying settles on a total, while enumerating counts the items off one by one until every single member is listed.
Measure means to find a thing's size or extent against a standard; quantify goes one step further — the result must come out as an explicit number, not just 'longer' or 'warmer.'
Calculate means to work a number out from other numbers by arithmetic; quantifying starts earlier, turning something unnumbered — fear, fog, loyalty — into figures a calculation could then use.
Gauge means to estimate an amount, often roughly and by instinct; you can gauge a crowd's mood in a glance, but to quantify it you would need a count.

The sleep researchers refused to accept 'the patients seem more rested' and set out to quantify it: minutes to fall asleep, number of wakings, hours of deep sleep — until restfulness had become a column of numbers.
That conversion is the whole verb: something real but unnumbered — restedness — gets measured and expressed as figures.
Quantify builds on Latin quantus, 'how much,' plus -ify, 'to make': literally, to make into a how-much.
Quantify is the verb of skeptics and scientists: it demands that a claim trade its adjectives for figures.
It shines with things that resist numbers — morale, risk, pain — and sounds redundant with things already numbered; nobody needs to quantify a price tag.
'Hard to quantify' is the phrase's natural habitat.
